rationale: One missing syscall, and every ingredient it needs already exists. sys_times is absent from the entire kernel -- a repo-wide grep for `sys_times`/`SYS_TIMES` in *.rs finds nothing, and both dispatch tables skip its number: kernel/src/syscall/arch/x86.rs jumps SYS_SYSINFO = 99 straight to SYS_PTRACE = 101 (no `= 100`), and kernel/src/syscall/arch/generic.rs has no `= 153`. Unknown numbers hit the `_ =>` arm in kernel/src/syscall/mod.rs:337 and return ENOSYS. The fix is additive and narrow: a handler that reads clocks and writes one 4-field struct, taking no locks beyond the ones procfs already takes, and touching no filesystem, scheduling, or memory state. All four `struct tms` fields are already computed elsewhere in tree -- kernel/src/fs/fs_impls/procfs/pid/task/stat.rs:180-196 builds exactly utime/stime from `process.prof_clock().user_clock().read_jiffies()` / `kernel_clock()` and cutime/cstime from `process.reaped_children_stats().lock().get()`, which is the same pairing sys_getrusage uses at kernel/src/syscall/getrusage.rs:26-52. The accounting is live, not stubbed: kernel/src/process/process/timer_manager.rs:66-71 ticks both the user and kernel CpuClock every jiffy, and kernel/src/process/wait.rs:342 accumulates reaped children, which is what makes the test's monotonicity and nonzero-cutime assertions satisfiable. Measured both sides myself rather than trusting the cache. Host (pinned LTP 20260529 prebuilt, /nix/store/hik6kb512ia3p14lc2vwzb292d4k306a-ltp-20260529): 12 passed / 0 failed, so the failure is Asterinas's and not the test's. Asterinas at base e8f2b9ca6, one boot probing 8 candidates: `times03: fail (7.757s)` while `times01: pass (0.000s)` in the same boot -- the split is itself informative and resolves an apparent contradiction I chased down. times01 is already enabled in all.txt line 1706 and green, which looked at first like evidence times() works; it does not. times01 only checks `TST_RET == -1`, and glibc's times() wrapper reports failure solely for EFAULT, so an ENOSYS return is not seen as -1 and times01 passes vacuously without ever inspecting the buffer. times03 reads the tms fields, so it is the first test that actually exercises the syscall -- which also means enabling it closes a real coverage hole rather than a cosmetic one. Preferred over the 6 other failures measured in the same boot, each broader or murkier: pathconf02 came back broken rather than merely failing, pointing at harness/setup trouble to untangle before any kernel defect is visible; getcpu01 needs per-CPU/NUMA node reporting; setitimer01 is interval-timer delivery (2.673s, timing-sensitive); waitpid01 is process-reaping semantics; chdir01 and fcntl27 sit in the VFS and file-locking paths that earlier rounds already worked over. Fresh ground for round 3: no committed branch touches CPU-time accounting for processes. Reviewed the diff of all 27 committed fix-ltp-* branches against e8f2b9ca6 -- the timer rounds touched timer_create.rs, timer_settime.rs, and timerfd_gettime.rs (POSIX/fd timers, not process CPU-time reporting), and clock_getres01 touched the clock resolution and vdso paths; none added a syscall that reports accumulated process times, and none touched procfs stat.rs or getrusage.rs.
notes: Pool entry is `# times03` at test/initramfs/src/conformance/ltp/testcases/all.txt line 1707; enable by uncommenting to `times03`. Sibling times01 is already enabled at line 1706 and passes (vacuously, per rationale) -- leave it alone. times03 appears in neither blocked/ext2.txt nor blocked/exfat.txt, so run_vars is empty: the default workdir (/tmp) with no extra blocklists, which is the configuration phase 4 verifies. Host baseline and the 8-candidate Asterinas probe are recorded in select.cache under run-Vr5gET. Static evidence for the missing syscall (absent from both tables, ENOSYS fallback at kernel/src/syscall/mod.rs:337) was confirmed by grep; I did not capture an `Unimplemented syscall number: 100` line from qemu.log, since that warning is emitted at a log level the conformance boot does not surface -- diagnose should confirm the ENOSYS path directly.
